text: Here's a mistake you'll actually meet, the name box that refuses Anna. Back to our contact form, the developer adds a name box above the message, and it gets its own state. Up near the top of ContactForm.jsx, there are now two state lines. Line four makes name with setName, starting as an empty string, and line five is the one we already had, message with setMessage, also starting empty. They remember from principle two that value lets send empty the box, but in the markup, they forget onChange. Further down in the same file, line twenty opens the form with onSubmit equals handleSend in curly braces, then a label, the word Name, and on line twenty-three, the input. It has value equals name in curly braces, and that's it. The note there says, "Wrong. No onChange," so every letter is put back. The user clicks into the name box and types Anna. The box stays empty, and the console has shown the error since the page opened. In figure seventeen, we zoom out. It's the whole contact form now, a heading, Contact Us, then an empty name box, a message box, the counter showing zero out of two hundred, and the Send button. No Anna anywhere. And down in the console, there's that same red line again about a value prop without an onChange handler and a read-only field. The steps are the same as for John. The browser shows each letter, no code saves it, and React writes the empty name back into the box. The fix is an onChange, like the one the message box already has. So on line twenty-three, the input gets a second prop. Next to value equals name, we add onChange, and in the curly braces, an arrow function. It takes e and calls setName with e.target.value. The note says it, each letter now reaches state. The send handler now logs the name, too, and empties it together with the message. That's handleSend starting on line eleven, and it takes e. Line twelve calls e.preventDefault, so the page doesn't reload. Line thirteen logs the word Sent, then Name, then Message, and then two setters. Line fourteen calls setName with an empty string, so the name box empties together with the message. And line fifteen calls setMessage with an empty string, like before. After a reload, Anna appears letter by letter, and the console is clean. Figure eighteen shows it. Same contact form, but now the name box says Anna, the message box is still empty, the counter still reads zero out of two hundred, and the console simply says, "No errors or warnings." The broken box and the fixed box look like the same box with one extra prop. They even show the same empty text when the page opens, but they are not the same. They split at step three. Only the fixed box saves the letter in state, so only its letters survive.
